key_concept: The Q value of a nuclear reaction is the mass defect converted to energy: $Q = (m_{\text{reactants}} - m_{\text{products}})c^2$, with $1\ u = 931.5\ MeV$.
steps: Write the Q value for the $\alpha$-decay: $Q = [m(^{238}U) - m(^{234}Th) - m(^{4}He)]c^2$.
Find the mass of the products: $234.043 + 4.003 = 238.046\ u$.
Find the mass defect: $\Delta m = 238.050 - 238.046 = 0.004\ u$.
Convert to keV: $3.726\ MeV = 3726\ keV$. Since $Q > 0$, the decay is energetically allowed (exoergic).
why_not_others: Options (2), (3) and (4) come from rounding $931.5$ to $932$ or $933.5$ ($0.004\times932 = 3728$) or from arithmetic slips. With the given conversion factor, only $3726\ keV$ is exact.
common_trap: Students forget to convert MeV to keV (multiply by $1000$), or they subtract the masses in the wrong order and get a negative Q.
time_saving_tip: Spot the mass defect $0.004\ u$ at once. Then $4 \times 931.5 = 3726$ gives the answer directly in keV, because $0.004\ u \times 931.5\ MeV/u = 4 \times 931.5\ keV$.
